patterns.rationale: Miss 1 uses a labeled "active" checkpoint trigger (Checkpoint VRTX-001 (active)) to register a deferred instruction. The `(active)` qualifier in parentheses after "checkpoint" is injection-specific formatting — legitimate deployment or incident-response checkpoints do not use this activation-state label format.
patterns.fp_notes: Deployment docs use "checkpoint" but not with `(active)` parenthetical — closest benign form would be "checkpoint: service is active" which doesn't match.

patterns.rationale: Miss 2 uses a YAML `deferred_action:` key to stage a conditional exfiltration step. This is not a standard key in any common YAML schema (Docker Compose, Kubernetes, GitHub Actions, Ansible); its presence in a document signals a custom injection-designed manifest. The sibling key `trigger_condition:` reinforces intent but `deferred_action` is the primary signal.
patterns.fp_notes: No standard CI/CD or plugin schema uses `deferred_action` as a key name.

patterns.rationale: Miss 4 frames the injection as a GDPR Article 22 "binding" directive from a "data controller." Real GDPR documentation says "the data controller is responsible for…" or "consent is legally binding" — it does not use "binding under [role] authority" as an imperative addressed to a processing agent. This phrasing is unique to authority-spoofing injections.
patterns.fp_notes: GDPR/legal policy docs use "data controller" and "binding" separately, not as `binding under data controller authority`; security_policy.md contains neither.

patterns.rationale: Miss 5 uses "forward" as a synonym for "send/post/submit" — all three of which are already blocked — to push runtime values to an HTTP endpoint. This pattern closes the lexical gap and is consistent with the existing `send.*to.*http`, `post.*to.*https?://`, and `submit.*to.*https?://` branches.
patterns.fp_notes: API reference docs may say "forward requests to https://api.example.com"; deployment guides may mention proxy forwarding to HTTPS backends. Acceptable given that all existing analogous patterns carry the same risk profile and the known-good corpus snippets do not contain this construction.

patterns.rationale: Miss 6 impersonates notebook infrastructure by using the heading "Notebook Processor Note" to make the injection appear to be a legitimate kernel directive. Real Jupyter/Colab documentation does not use this term — actual infrastructure metadata appears as cell metadata JSON or `%magic` commands, never as a prose header claiming to be a "processor note."
patterns.fp_notes: Legitimate ML notebooks have setup cells and markdown headings, but not a "Notebook Processor Note" section header; "notebook" and "processor" co-occur in legitimate docs (e.g., NLP pipelines) but not in this compound heading form.

patterns.rationale: Miss 6 substitutes "relay" for "send/transmit" and "runtime tokens" for "credentials/secrets" to evade the existing `transmit.*credential` branch. "Relay" has legitimate meanings in networking (DHCP relay, message relay) but "relay runtime token" specifically — where "runtime token" denotes an auth credential — is injection vocabulary; legitimate networking docs that discuss relay do not use the term "runtime token."
patterns.fp_notes: Networking docs use "relay" frequently but pair it with addresses/packets, not "runtime token"; the known-good debug_guide.md discusses agent logs and session tokens but not "relay."
